issues.legal_issue: A decree is a nullity for execution purposes only when it was passed by a court lacking inherent jurisdiction, not merely because the court made an error.
material_facts: An eviction decree was passed by a court in a suit brought under rent-control legislation.
The tenant challenged the decree’s executability in execution, alleging that the court had not established the statutory grounds for eviction.
issues.conclusion: The decree was not a nullity merely because of an alleged error in passing it; a decree is a nullity only if it is beyond the powers of the court that passed it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court generally must execute the decree and cannot go behind it unless it is a nullity. A decree is a nullity when the court lacked inherent jurisdiction, rather than when the decree is merely erroneous or voidable.

predicates.execution_challenge: A judgment-debtor challenged the decree’s validity or executability in execution proceedings.
predicates.court_had_inherent_jurisdiction: The court that passed the decree had inherent authority to decide the kind of dispute before it.
predicates.decree_alleged_erroneous: The judgment-debtor alleged that the court made an error in passing the decree.

issues.definition: When a decree is challenged in execution, an alleged error does not make it a nullity if the court had inherent authority to pass it.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise eviction decree under rent-control legislation may be valid when the compromise and case record provide material from which the court’s satisfaction about statutory eviction grounds can be inferred.
material_facts: The landlord sued for eviction on statutory grounds that included rent arrears and bona fide personal requirement.
The tenant’s pleadings disputed the arrears and the landlord’s personal requirement, but the tenant admitted the demand notice had been received.
In written compromise terms, the tenant admitted the claimed arrears and referred to amounts deposited in court; the record contained no evidence of a tender of rent before the suit.
The tenant agreed to deliver possession at a later time for accommodation, and the court recorded that the parties admitted the compromise.
The decree was challenged during execution as lacking material establishing statutory grounds for eviction.
issues.conclusion: The compromise terms and the record supported implied admissions of the statutory eviction grounds, so the decree was not a nullity and was executable.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to eviction proceedings under the rent-control legislation, which did not prohibit compromise. The court’s satisfaction that a statutory ground exists may be inferred from the compromise, pleadings, and other material; express findings or evidence on the merits are not always necessary. A tenant’s clear judicial admission is binding and may supply the material for that satisfaction. The Court relied on K.K. Chari v. R.M. Sheshadhri, Nagindass v. Dalpatram, Roshan Lal v. Madan Lal, and Suleman Noormohammed v. Umarbhai; it also referred to Section 58 of the Evidence Act. The relevant statutory grounds were under Sections 12(3)(a), 13(1)(g), and 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and compromise_decree and arrears_admitted_in_compromise and no_prior_tender_recorded and tenant_agreed_to_vacate_later

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on grounds governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.compromise_decree: The court passed an eviction decree based on written compromise terms accepted by the parties.
predicates.arrears_admitted_in_compromise: The tenant admitted in the compromise that the claimed rent arrears were due.
predicates.no_prior_tender_recorded: The case record contained no material showing that the tenant had tendered the demanded rent before the suit.
predicates.tenant_agreed_to_vacate_later: The tenant agreed to give up possession at a later time, receiving time or accommodation before doing so.

issues.definition: A compromise eviction decree is executable where an eviction proceeding ends in a compromise that admits arrears, the record shows no prior tender, and the tenant agrees to vacate later.

issues.legal_issue: An executing court deciding whether a decree is a nullity must examine the record on which the decree was based and may not permit the parties to introduce fresh evidence on that objection.
material_facts: The tenant objected in execution that the compromise eviction decree was a nullity.
The executing court allowed the tenant to produce documentary evidence to support the objection.
issues.conclusion: Allowing the tenant to lead fresh evidence in execution was unwarranted; the executing court had to assess nullity from the record on which the decree was based.
issues.legal_principle: An executing court may examine the decree and the original record to determine whether material supported the court’s authority to pass it, but it cannot sit as an appellate court or permit fresh evidence to relitigate the issue. This principle was applied consistently with the Court’s discussion of Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and its reliance on Nagindass v. Dalpatram.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court was asked to enforce a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_challenged_as_nullity: The judgment-debtor contended in execution that the decree was a nullity.
predicates.party_seeks_fresh_evidence: A party sought permission to introduce evidence that was not part of the record on which the decree was based.

issues.definition: When a judgment-debtor challenges a decree as a nullity in execution and a party seeks fresh evidence, the executing court must decide the challenge from the existing record.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord suing for eviction on bona fide personal requirement need not plead comparative hardship in the plaint as a prerequisite to bringing the suit.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of bona fide personal requirement.
The tenant pleaded that greater hardship would result to the tenant if eviction were ordered.
The High Court treated the absence of a pleading about the landlord’s comparative hardship as relevant to the decree’s validity.
issues.conclusion: The landlord was not required to plead comparative hardship in the plaint; that question arises after the court is satisfied that the bona fide personal-requirement ground has been established.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 13(1)(g) and 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the court considers comparative hardship at the stage after it is satisfied that bona fide personal requirement has been established. Comparative-hardship averments are therefore not required in the plaint to create the cause of action for eviction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.bona_fide_requirement_ground_claimed: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the premises were reasonably and bona fide required for occupation.
predicates.comparative_hardship_considered_at_later: The governing procedure considers comparative hardship only after the court is satisfied that the bona fide-requirement ground is established.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction suit based on bona fide requirement, the landlord need not plead comparative hardship when that question is considered only at a later stage.
